name: encapsulate-collection
intent: Keep a collection field private to the object that owns it and publish only behaviour over it - a read-only view, a copy or an iterator for reads, explicit add and remove operations for membership changes - so that no client can change what is in the collection without the owner knowing.
problem: An object stores a collection of children (lines, employees, courses, subscribers) and exposes it through an ordinary getter/setter: callers add, remove or clear elements behind the owner's back, so validation is skipped, derived state (counts, totals, indexes, change events) silently goes stale, and the owner can no longer state any invariant about who may join or leave the collection.
context: Applies wherever an object owns a collection whose membership is part of its contract - aggregates, order/invoice/document objects, registries, subscriber lists, tree nodes - and is most urgent in languages where a collection is a reference type (Java, C#, Kotlin, Scala, JavaScript/TypeScript objects, Go slices, Smalltalk) and where the owner keeps derived state or fires notifications on change. It is a local, per-class API decision independent of any framework, and it is orthogonal to concurrency: the pattern decides who may change membership, not how concurrent access is serialised.
benefits: Membership changes have exactly one path, so validation, derived state (counts, sums, caches) and notifications stay consistent by construction.
Clients can read the collection without acquiring the ability to change it, which removes a whole class of accidental corruption (a stray push/append/add on the returned object).
The public API promises capabilities, not representation: the field can move from list to set to sorted structure, or be split, without touching callers.
Invariants about the collection - uniqueness, ordering, non-null elements, parent pointers, ownership - become enforceable at all, since the owner sees every transition.
The published read contract (view vs copy vs iterator) can be chosen per consumer and documented once, instead of being inherited accidentally from the field's type.
Tests and clients get a narrower seam: they exercise add/remove and the read interface rather than constructing situations that depend on the concrete container type.
tradeoffs: The API grows and bulk operations lose their shorthand: adding ten elements is ten calls unless the owner also publishes an explicit bulk operation (addAll/replaceAll).

Live read-only views (Collections.unmodifiableList, ReadOnlyCollection<T>, Kotlin List over a MutableList) report violations at call time via UnsupportedOperationException/NotSupportedException rather than at compile time, and keep changing under the caller when the owner mutates the collection.
Defensive copies allocate on every read and are shallow - they protect membership, not the elements, whose mutation still leaks through the shared references.

Returning an iterator avoids the copy but withholds size, contains and random access, and fails fast (ConcurrentModificationException, frozen enumerators) when the collection changes during iteration.

The published interface is a promise: a signature naming a mutable collection type (List<T>, MutableList, MutableArray) documents the right to mutate it, so choosing read-only types may cost a per-call wrapper allocation or force an immutable backing store.

The discipline is only as strong as its weakest escape hatch: one leftover accessor, reflective/serialization hook or framework that insists on the raw collection (GUI data binding is the classic case) reinstates the original bug.
Encapsulated membership is not thread-safety: concurrent add/remove still needs synchronisation owned by the object, and a caller iterating a live view can observe a torn state.

participants.responsibility: The object that holds the collection: decides the representation, keeps the field private, publishes the read contract and the membership operations, and enforces the invariants plus any derived state that depends on membership.
The published read path - a read-only view, a defensive copy or an iterator - that lets clients see the elements without reaching the mutable container that stores them.
Explicit add/remove (and optionally bulk replace) methods that accept elements rather than whole collections, validate them, update derived state and are the only paths that may change membership.
Reads through the accessor and changes membership through the operations; it never holds the underlying container and therefore cannot bypass the owner's rules.
The encapsulated storage itself - its concrete type is an implementation detail the owner is free to change.

use_cases: Aggregate roots that own child entities (Order → OrderLines, Invoice → LineItems): lines are added and removed through the root so totals, discounts and invariants stay correct.
Records with a many-valued field (Person → courses, Company → employees): membership changes must be validated and may need to update indexes or raise domain events.
Subscriber/observer registries where register and unregister must be intercepted to start or stop notifications and to avoid duplicate subscriptions.
Tree or document nodes holding children, where adding or removing a child must set or clear the parent back-pointer and keep the node's cached size consistent.
Configuration objects that accumulate values (plugins, interceptors, allowed origins) and publish them read-only to the framework that consumes them.
Scene graphs, sprite groups or UI container objects where attach/detach must trigger lifecycle hooks on the owners of the elements.
Domain-Driven Design aggregates: aggregate roots own entity collections and enforce invariants; the repository pattern returns the aggregate but the aggregate itself enforces all membership rules.

Event-sourcing projections: projectors hold a collection of events to replay; the collection must be encapsulated so replay order and state derivation are controlled, not interleaved with external mutations.

Plugin or extension registries: a host application loads plugins and stores them; adding/removing plugins must update the registry's internal loader state, fire lifecycle events, and potentially recompile an index.

GUI data-binding scenarios (Fowler's sticky case): a framework binds a UI control directly to a collection property; in this case use the framework's observable/read-only collection wrapper (ObservableCollection<T> in .NET, ObservableList in JavaFX) as the published read path rather than a bare unmodifiable wrapper.

Caching layers that accumulate entries (LRU cache, memoisation table): the cache owner must control eviction policy; exposing the internal map/list lets callers bypass eviction and cause memory leaks or policy violations.

Hibernate ORM entities: persistent collection-valued fields are declared as interfaces and swapped for lazy, change-detecting wrappers owned by the entity; @Immutable on a mapped collection makes any external add/remove/clear throw HibernateException at flush instead of silently rewriting child rows.

Google Guava as the published read path: ImmutableSet/ImmutableList.copyOf and ImmutableXXX.Builder give an owner a null-rejecting snapshot to hand out, preferred in Guava's own guidance over a live unmodifiable wrapper because the published value cannot drift while callers hold it.

Kotlin standard library convention: keep the MutableList private and publish the read-only List interface; the read-only/mutable interface split makes the encapsulation a compile-time fact rather than a runtime UnsupportedOperationException, and buildList()/toList() provide the snapshot variant.
avoid_when: The object is a plain data carrier (DTO, record, tuple) whose collection has no invariants: an immutable record with a read-only field, or the language's own value semantics, is simpler.
The collection is genuinely public state - an in-memory buffer or a bag with no rules about membership - where wrapping only adds ceremony.
A framework demands direct access to the collection for binding or serialization and no interception is needed: use that framework's observable/read-only mechanism instead of hand-written accessors.

A performance-critical inner loop cannot pay a per-read copy and an iterator's restricted API does not fit: hand out a borrowed read-only view (&[T], std::span, ReadOnlySpan, ReadonlyArray) rather than copying.
The type is a short-lived local working structure (a task-scoped accumulator): module-level functions that return the collection are easier to read than a class that guards it.
anti_patterns: Getter returns the live collection: the field is private but the accessor leaks the container, so clients add and remove as if it were public state.
Setter takes a whole collection — setCourses(list) — which replaces membership wholesale and skips validation, bookkeeping and notifications.
Read-only view over a field the owner keeps mutating: callers receive UnsupportedOperationException or ConcurrentModificationException at unpredictable moments instead of a stable read.

Encapsulation by comment: returning the field (or a frozen copy of it) with 'do not modify' in the docs, or relying on Python's underscore / TypeScript's erased private keyword, provides no enforcement at all.
Protecting the container but not the elements: a frozen or unmodifiable list of mutable objects still shares those objects, so element mutation leaks through the abstraction.
Iterator-only access: publishing traversal while callers need size/contains/index forces them to escape the abstraction or rebuild it from scratch.

Live ReadOnlyCollection in C#: ReadOnlyCollection<T> is a view over the original IList — if the owner mutates the underlying list, the view reflects those changes immediately; callers who expect a stable snapshot are surprised.

Constructor reference leak (Java): passing a mutable collection into the constructor and storing the reference directly lets the caller mutate the object's state after construction, even though the field is private; must copy in the constructor.

Returning ICollection<T> in C#: the interface includes Add, Remove, Clear; callers who access the collection through the interface can invoke these methods and cause NotSupportedException at runtime — prefer IReadOnlyCollection<T> or return the concrete ReadOnlyCollection<T> directly.

Yield-return IEnumerable<T> as snapshot: in C#, yield return over a LINQ query re-executes the query on every foreach; callers who expect a stable collection are misled; a materialized ReadOnlyCollection<T> is the correct snapshot type.

Confusing view with snapshot in Java: Collections.unmodifiableList wraps the original (mutations propagate to the view); List.copyOf() takes a snapshot (subsequent source mutations do not propagate); choosing the wrong one for a getter return value causes inconsistent state.

Shallow defensive copy: copying a List copies the container, not the elements — mutable elements are still shared references; callers can mutate them and affect the owner's state; document whether element immutability is a precondition.

Serialization bypasses getter: many serializers (JSON, XML, some ORM frameworks) access fields directly via reflection, bypassing getter/setter logic entirely; test the serialization path with a collection mutation to verify encapsulation holds.
design_principles: Information hiding: the collection's representation is an implementation detail; only capabilities (read, add, remove) are published.
Encapsulation as invariant enforcement: the owner, not the client, controls membership transitions - Tell-Don't-Ask applied to collections.
Single responsibility: the rules about who may join or leave the collection live with the object whose state depends on them.
Separation of concerns: reading and changing membership are different capabilities with different contracts, and are published separately.
Least privilege: clients receive the weakest access that satisfies them - a read-only view, a copy or an iterator rather than a mutable container.
best_practices: Initialise the field to an empty collection in the constructor so no later code has to null-check it.
Publish add/remove (and an explicit replaceAll/addAll when bulk use is real); never a setter that installs a collection the owner did not build.
Choose the read contract per consumer and document it: live view when callers must see updates, snapshot copy when they must be isolated, iterator when only traversal is needed.
Make the field private/module-private and treat every escape hatch (raw getter, serialization hook, framework binding, reflective access) as a reviewed exception.
Where a per-read copy is too expensive, hand out a borrowed read-only view (const&, std::span, ReadOnlySpan, &[T], ReadonlyArray) instead of copying.
Enforce with the type system where it exists (List vs MutableList, IReadOnlyList, readonly T[], private(set)) and test the negative case: a mutation attempt must fail.
Keep the element type immutable, or state explicitly that the pattern protects membership and not the elements.

Java: prefer List.copyOf() (snapshot, truly immutable) over Collections.unmodifiableList() (live view over a mutable source) for getter return values; use Collections.unmodifiableList() only when the owner genuinely owns the source and will not mutate it after publication.
Java records with mutable component collections require a compact constructor that copies via List.copyOf(); the compiler does not insert defensive copies automatically.
Java: in constructors, copy the argument collection via new ArrayList<>(input) or List.copyOf() before storing — passing a reference lets the caller mutate the collection after construction.

C#: return ReadOnlyCollection<T> (not ICollection<T> — the interface still carries mutating methods that throw NotSupportedException when called through the interface); IReadOnlyList<T> / IReadOnlyCollection<T> are preferred interface return types.
C#: use private(set) on the property declaration to make mutation only possible inside the owner, while still allowing read access from outside.

C#: avoid yield return IEnumerable<T> for collection access unless you genuinely want a snapshot per enumeration — repeated enumeration may re-execute queries; prefer ReadOnlyCollection<T> for consistent read semantics.

Python: use @property to wrap a private list; return tuple(self._items) or list(self._items) for a copy; tuple signals immutability to callers; namedtuple or dataclass(frozen=True) for truly immutable element types.
Kotlin: expose only List (read-only interface) publicly; keep MutableList as the internal type; this enforces read-only access at compile time rather than runtime.
Go: return a slice copy (append([]T(nil), s...)) or a pointer to a slice header (used rarely); prefer functional options pattern for construction to avoid exposing the internal slice.

Serialization compatibility: ReadOnlyCollection<T> (C#) and Collections.unmodifiableList (Java) are serialisable in most frameworks without special handling; defensive copies are generally NOT serialisable unless the elements are — test the serialization path explicitly.
sources: Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code (1999; 2nd ed. 2018) — 'Encapsulate Collection' refactoring (Organizing Data): a getter must not return the collection itself; add/remove operations replace the setter.

https://martinfowler.com/bliki/EncapsulatedCollection.html — Fowler's bliki post (2004) explaining protection proxy, copy, and iterator as the three read-path options; emphasises that get/set works for single values but breaks encapsulation for collections.

https://martinfowler.com/ieeeSoftware/dataAccessRoutines.pdf — Fowler, 'Data Access Routines', IEEE Software, Nov 2003 (https://doi.org/10.1109/MS.2003.1241375): definitive technical treatment of single-value vs collection encapsulation; covers protection proxy (preferred), defensive copy, and iterator; warns against convention-only protection and GUI framework binding trade-offs.
https://refactoring.com/catalog/encapsulateCollection.html — Official refactoring.com catalog entry with JavaScript/TypeScript code sketch showing .slice() on the getter.

https://refactoring.guru/encapsulate-collection — Step-by-step refactoring procedure; explains why setters should be renamed to replaceAll rather than removed entirely; notes arrays need element-wise methods while standard collections restrict access to unwanted mutators.

https://www.informit.com/store/smalltalk-best-practice-patterns-9780132852111 — Beck, Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns (1997): collection encapsulation idioms including Composed Method applied to add/remove, and the Buck'Adopted Child' pattern for parent-pointer back-links.

https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/collections/implementations/wrapper.html — Java Tutorials: 'Wrapper Implementations' covering Collections.unmodifiableList (protection proxy) vs List.copyOf() (snapshot); distinction between live view and true immutable copy.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/ca2227 — Microsoft CA2227: 'Collection properties should be read-only' — writable collection properties allow wholesale replacement; fix is read-only or init-only property plus Clear/AddRange pattern; concurrent collections as thread-safe read-only return type.

http://javapractices.com/topic/TopicAction.do?Id=173 — Java Practices Topic 173: Encapsulate collections — shows correct form (Collections.unmodifiableSet in getter, defensive copy in constructor) vs the broken form (direct field reference) with explanation of why ORM-generated getters are dangerous.

https://blog.frankel.ch/back-to-basics-encapsulating-collections/ — Frankel (2014): constructor argument defensive copy is mandatory — passing a reference in the constructor lets the caller mutate the collection after construction; correct form copies the argument via addAll.

https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/main/docs/standard/design-guidelines/guidelines-for-collections.md — .NET Design Guidelines for Collections: snapshot vs live collections; properties must return live collections (no per-read copy); IReadOnlyCollection<T> and ReadOnlyCollection<T> as read-only return types; choose Collection<T> for read-write, ReadOnlyCollection<T> for read-only.

https://www.resumelens.org/blog/java/java-immutability-and-defensive-copying — Java immutability deep dive: List.copyOf() vs Collections.unmodifiableList() (snapshot vs live view); shallow defensive copy leaves mutable elements exposed; records with mutable components need compact constructors.

https://github.com/google/guava/wiki/ImmutableCollectionsExplained — Guava wiki: immutable collections as defensive-by-default copies (copyOf/of/Builder), the null-rejection policy, and the rationale for preferring ImmutableXXX over live unmodifiable wrappers as the published read path.

https://docs.hibernate.org/orm/6.2/javadocs/org/hibernate/annotations/Immutable.html — Hibernate @Immutable: a collection marked immutable rejects add/remove/clear with a HibernateException at flush, enforcing collection encapsulation at the persistence layer; companion guidance in the user guide (https://docs.hibernate.org/orm/5.2/userguide/html_single/chapters/domain/immutability.html).

https://kotlinlang.org/docs/collections-overview.html — Kotlin collections overview: read-only Collection/List/Set versus MutableCollection/MutableList/MutableSet; a MutableList referenced through the read-only interface cannot be mutated through that reference — compile-time encapsulation, but the underlying object remains mutable (read-only is not immutable).

https://blog.kdgregory.com/2011/10/defensive-copies-are-code-smell.html — Criticism of reflexive defensive copying: the memory/CPU cost of copying internal state on every read, and the argument that moving behaviour into the owner (Law of Demeter) often removes the need to publish the collection at all.

related_patterns_notes.memento: captures collection state as an immutable snapshot for undo/redo; complements the pattern's add/remove operations by recording the before-state.
related_patterns_notes.proxy: the protection proxy (Collections.unmodifiableList, ReadOnlyCollection<T>) is literally a Proxy pattern applied to the collection accessor; the wrapper intercepts mutation attempts.
related_patterns_notes.observer: collection change events (CollectionChanged in .NET, ObservableList in JavaFX) are an Observer applied to collection mutation; the owner publishes add/remove notifications when membership changes.
related_patterns_notes.facade: a collection accessor simplifies the internal collection structure (a set vs a sorted list vs a tree) and presents a uniform read interface to callers.
related_patterns_notes.flyweight: when collection elements are shared references (as in a scene graph or file-system tree), the flyweight pattern explains why element identity matters and parent back-pointers must be maintained consistently.
related_patterns_notes.builder: bulk population of an encapsulated collection (addAll / replaceAll) is often implemented via a builder that stages elements before committing them to the owner in one operation.
